extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers of Kant
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the fundamental principles, distinctions, and limits of practical reason (moral philosophy), especially the distinction between maxims and laws, hypothetical and categorical imperatives, and the role of freedom and postulates in practical thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of practical principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical principles are propositions which contain a general determination of the will, having under it several practical rules. They are subjective, or maxims, when the condition is regarded by the subject as valid only for his own will, but are objective, or practical laws, when the condition is recognized as objective, that is, valid for the will of every rational being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes maxims (subjective principles) from practical laws (objective principles). Use this distinction to judge whether a principle is merely a personal rule or a universal law binding on all rational beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperatives vs. maxims (objective necessitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperatives are rules characterized by 'shall,' which express the objective necessitation of the action and signify that, if reason completely determined the will, the action would inevitably take place according to this rule. Maxims are principles, but not imperatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate whether a directive counts as law rather than mere guidance, check whether it expresses objective necessitation ('shall') and would determine the will independently of contingent subjective conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical imperatives (precepts of skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperatives which are conditional — i.e., do not determine the will simply as will, but only in respect to a desired effect — are hypothetical imperatives and contain mere precepts of skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothetical imperatives prescribe means relative to an end (e.g., be industrious to avoid want in old age). They are not moral laws because their necessity depends on contingent desires or ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical imperative (practical law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperatives that determine the will as will, independent of desired effects, are categorical and would alone be practical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true moral law must be categorical: it must command unconditionally and determine the will prior to consideration of empirical ends or subjective desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of universality and a priori status for laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws must be sufficient to determine the will as will, without presupposing contingent subjective conditions; hence they must be a priori and universally valid across rational beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess candidate principles for (1) independence from empirical matters of desire and (2) applicability to all rational beings — if either fails, the principle is not a genuine practical law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem I — material presupposition defeats lawhood
rubrics_metrics.description: All practical principles which presuppose an object (matter) of the faculty of desire as the ground of determination of the will are empirical and can furnish no practical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a principle depends on the existence of some desired object or the subject's susceptibility to pleasure/pain, it is material/empirical and cannot serve as an objective practical law. Example: rules grounded in expected pleasure are empirical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem II — material practical principles reduce to self-love
rubrics_metrics.description: All material practical principles as such are of one and the same kind and come under the general principle of self-love or private happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material (object/pleasure-based) principles ultimately aim at private happiness; identifying this shows their empirical character and lack of moral authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary — lower desires as determinant in material rules
rubrics_metrics.description: All material practical rules place the determining principle of the will in the lower desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a diagnostic: if a rule's motivating ground is lower desires (pleasure, self-interest), it is not a moral law but a material practical rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rule as product of reason prescribing means
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical rule is always a product of reason, because it prescribes action as a means to the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish rules that reason formulates instrumentally (how to achieve ends) from laws that determine the will itself; the former are often hypothetical imperatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction in modality: permitted/forbidden vs duty/contrary to duty
rubrics_metrics.description: In the table of categories of Practical reason under Modality, the Permitted and forbidden (possible and impossible in a practical objective point of view) differ from duty and contrary to duty. The former mean what coincides with or contradicts a merely possible practical precept; the latter relate to a law actually present in reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating actions, separate what is merely permitted/forbidden as practically possible from what is required or opposed to a law of reason (duty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of presupposing reason itself for lawhood
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason gives laws only if it needs to presuppose itself, because rules are objectively and universally valid only when they hold without any contingent subjective conditions which distinguish one rational being from another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine moral law must be grounded in pure practical reason itself, not in contingent empirical features of agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulates of pure practical reason as necessary hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas such as God and immortality are postulates of pure practical reason: their possibility must be assumed for practical purposes (e.g., to secure the summum bonum), not because we can theoretically prove them; they are necessary hypotheses for the subject's obedience to moral law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat postulates as practically necessary but not apodeictically established; they serve pragmatic roles in moral theory and ought not be conflated with theoretical certainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom as condition and ratio essendi of moral law
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom is the condition (ratio essendi) of the moral law; the moral law is the ratio cognoscendi of freedom. The reality of the concept of freedom is proved by an apodeictic law of practical reason and is the keystone for attributing objective reality to ideas like God and immortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral claims, recognize that freedom is posited as the prerequisite that makes moral obligation intelligible; arguments about moral obligation may depend on this transcendental conception of freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic method for practical reason: principles before concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: In critiquing practical reason we must commence with the principles (law of causality from freedom) and proceed to the concepts and then to the senses — the order is reverse of the critique of pure speculative reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologically, assess moral theories by first ascertaining their foundational practical principles (a priori), then deriving concepts and applications; do not start from empirical cases when seeking principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of critique: set principles not special duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The critique of practical reason's business is to assign in a complete manner the principles of its possibility, extent, and limits, without special reference to human nature; classification and specification of duties belong to systematic practical science, not to critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the critique to judge the validity and scope of principles (form and authority), but not as a rubric for enumerating particular human duties without further empirical or systematic inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prejudging via empirical definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical precaution: not to prejudge questions by adventuring definitions before the notion has been completely analysed (e.g., not to define faculty of desire in a way that makes moral principle empirical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating moral arguments, ensure definitions do not covertly import empirical assumptions that would undermine a priori status of moral laws.
